title: Which data quality tool fits you?

questions.q: What job do you want the tool to do?
questions.hint: The post says data quality tools do three different jobs, so start here.

options.label: Run rules I write in a pipeline
options.why: you want rules you write and run in a pipeline

options.label: Watch production tables for surprises
options.why: you want something to watch tables for drift

options.label: A free catalog with quality tests too
options.why: you want a catalog with tests built in

options.label: Cleansing and governance across a big company
options.why: you need profiling, cleansing and governance

questions.q: What does your data stack look like?

options.label: We already transform data with dbt
Our data runs on Apache Spark
No dbt and no Spark, we write Python
options.why: dbt tests need dbt and Deequ needs Spark

options.label: $0 for now
options.why: it has a free plan or free software

options.label: I can pay, but I want a price I can see
A sales quote is fine
options.why: its paid plans are quote based

options.label: A vendor hosts it
options.why: it is sold as a hosted platform or cloud service

options.label: A small team that wants to start fast
options.why: our read is that small teams gain most from a few rules, then alerts

options.label: Large or regulated
options.why: our read is that large or regulated companies often begin on the catalog and governance side or need many tables watched

gx.name: Great Expectations
gx.summary: A free Python library for data tests (GX Core).
gx.bestWhen: You want rules written in Python that you can review and version like code.
gx.watchOut: You write every rule yourself in Python. GX Cloud is no longer publicly available, per GX's May 2026 post, and the same post says Fivetran will become the new steward of GX Core.

soda.name: Soda
soda.summary: Checks written in YAML, with a free plan and a published Team price.
soda.bestWhen: You want an openly priced paid plan or a free hosted tier.
soda.watchOut: Soda Core uses the Elastic License 2.0, not Apache or MIT, and Soda's docs say Soda Core has no observability features. Those come from the hosted product.

dbt.name: dbt tests
dbt.summary: Tests built into dbt, such as unique, not_null, accepted_values and relationships.
dbt.bestWhen: You already transform your data with dbt.
dbt.watchOut: It only tests what dbt manages, and the docs we read do not describe cleansing or learned alerts.

elementary.name: Elementary
elementary.summary: An open-source tool that turns dbt test results into a report and alerts.
elementary.bestWhen: You use dbt and want a report and alerts on your dbt test results.
elementary.watchOut: The docs say the open-source tool covers a single dbt project, and it depends on dbt. Cloud plans say "Talk to us" instead of a price.

deequ.name: Deequ
deequ.summary: A free AWS Labs library that runs unit tests for data on Spark.
deequ.bestWhen: Your data is very large and already on Apache Spark.
deequ.watchOut: You need a Spark setup and a matching Java version. It is a library from AWS Labs, not an AWS managed service.

openmetadata.name: OpenMetadata
openmetadata.summary: A free open-source catalog with no-code quality tests and alerts.
openmetadata.bestWhen: You want one free tool for the catalog and the tests.
openmetadata.watchOut: You run and upgrade it yourself unless you use a managed offering, and it is more than a test library.

montecarlo.name: Monte Carlo
montecarlo.summary: A paid platform that monitors tables and traces issues.
montecarlo.bestWhen: Many tables across a company need watching and you can pay.
montecarlo.watchOut: No price is published, no free trial is mentioned and its pricing and platform pages show no open-source edition.

enterprise.name: Informatica or Ataccama
enterprise.summary: Enterprise suites for profiling, cleansing and governance.
enterprise.bestWhen: You need cleansing and governance across many teams in an enterprise suite.
enterprise.watchOut: Neither shows a dollar price on its own pages, and both are proprietary enterprise suites.
